title: Headed clearances are rising significantly – football should not ignore the health risks
content:
A couple of weeks ago, two football stories which seemed unrelated were, in reality, very much connected.

The first story was Arsenal’s apparent inability to score goals from open play, in the aftermath of their 3-2 defeat by Manchester United.

The second was the inquest into the death of former Scotland and Manchester United defender Gordon McQueen, who passed away in 2023 at the age of 70.

The latter, clearly, is of greater importance. It wasn’t simply about McQueen. The report from senior coroner Jonathan Heath was stark about the impact repeatedly heading footballs had upon his life, and indeed upon his death.

“I have found that Mr McQueen suffered repetitive head impacts during his career,” read the report. “I am satisfied on the balance of probability that repeatedly heading footballs contributed to his developing chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). The combination of CTE and vascular dementia led to pneumonia. I find the cause of death pneumonia, vascular dementia and CTE. It is likely that repetitive head impacts, sustained by heading the ball while playing football, contributed to the CTE.”

McQueen was an outstanding centre-back, and the subdeck on his Guardian obituary noted that he was “renowned for his heading skills”.

The position he played, at the heart of the defence, is of relevance.

Perhaps the key voice in the debate about heading is Professor Willie Stewart, who has previously asked football to consider whether heading is strictly necessary in the game. Stewart has found that goalkeepers — who rarely head the ball — develop CTE symptoms at a rate roughly in line with the general population, whereas for outfielders it is higher than in the general population. And it’s especially higher among defenders, who are tasked with making the most number of headers, both in defending their own box and — to a lesser but presumably still significant extent — when going forward for set pieces.

That brings us back to the first story.

By concentrating on a lack of open-play goals, the real message was that Arsenal were overly reliant on set pieces. But it’s really not just about Arsenal; it’s everyone.

It’s simply that Arsenal are the current Premier League leaders, and it feels unusual for the country’s best side to be so reliant on set pieces. Goals from dead-ball situations aren’t always about heading the ball — see Bryan Mbeumo rounding off a lovely move for Manchester United’s opener against Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday or Dominic Szoboszlai’s swerving free kick for Liverpool against Manchester City a day later — but Arsenal’s deliveries are generally about powerfully whipping the ball into the box, usually for centre-back Gabriel to head towards goal.

Up and down the Premier League, set pieces have taken on added importance.

Ahead of a meeting with Brentford this season, Crystal Palace manager Oliver Glasner admitted that his side’s training sessions had almost solely been about working on set pieces. The game, a 2-0 win for Palace, featured a goal from a long free kick, then one from a long throw-in. The match was, as a spectacle, terrible.

But that’s a matter of taste. This is also a matter of health.

The official Football Association guidance about heading recommends “a maximum number of 10 higher-force headers per training week”, and classifies ‘higher-force’ headers as those following a long ball (roughly 35m or more, such as when meeting a long goal kick), or, maybe more significantly, headers from corners, crosses or free kicks. If teams are focusing almost solely on set pieces in training, it’s fair to assume that (at least) some players will be performing far more than 10 higher-force headers a week in those sessions.

That definition more-or-less correlates with what Opta considers ‘headed clearances’. And using those numbers, we can observe how much the game has changed over the past two years, and the extent to which the rate of ‘higher-force headers’ has increased. In the Premier League, there are around 50 per cent more headed clearances now than two years ago, but in League Two, the fourth tier of English football, it’s nearly a 100 per cent increase.

That’s significant.

The lower leagues are sometimes considered to always have been about old-school football, about long balls and getting it in the mixer. That’s not the case. They’d basically fallen into line with the Premier League, and many teams in those divisions were previously trying to play tiki-taka. Anecdotally, the reversion to more basic football has been inspired by the Premier League big boys showing it is ‘acceptable’.

A couple of years back, Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola started fielding four centre-backs across the defence. They were, at least, highly technical players, and were supplemented with some of the world’s best creative players in the positions ahead of them. The copycats in the lower leagues can’t rely on that, and the football has become distinctly more old-school, with many more headers per game than, say, five years ago. It has a snowball effect: one club beef up their team with more aerial weapons, so others have to reciprocate in order to compete, and the process continues.

It should be noted that McQueen’s career ended in the mid-1980s, and he was playing with different footballs than the players of today.

Although the official weight of footballs has remained consistent throughout the sport’s history, those in McQueen’s era tended to collect water and become heavier in wet weather. But as his daughter Hayley, a Sky Sports television reporter, pointed out in the aftermath of the coroner’s report being released, modern footballs tend to be struck harder, and therefore travel faster, so the game should not be complacent about the risk to players today.

One suggestion to limit the impact of headers is to restrict them to the penalty areas only.

In percentage terms, there has been a slight shift towards this anyway, at least at Premier League level — 32 per cent in the boxes, compared to 26 per cent in 2019-19. This is probably a consequence of more sides playing out from the back at goal kicks, and also more emphasis being placed on long throw-ins recently.

Of course, the percentage difference can’t be considered in isolation; headers are happening more.

And all this has — or should have — changed the debate.

A few years ago, it was reasonable to suspect that heading was becoming less prevalent in football. That didn’t mean being blasé about the risks, but if the prototype for a centre-forward was Roberto Firmino rather than Andy Carroll, teams would adjust accordingly and aerial duels would be contested less regularly. That seemed the direction of travel.

This shift back towards old-school football has come out of nowhere.

The FA is not ignorant of the risks of heading. It was ahead of the curve on banning headers at youth levels of the game. And its study into the dangers of heading is well-researched, arrives at decent conclusions, and is available for everyone to read.

Those recommendations were published in 2021.

Five years seems recent enough — but the data shows quite how different football is today.
